To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) we developed allometric equations to estimate individual-tree bole and component biomass for a 10-year-old Douglas-fur plantation in southwestern Washington, (2) these equations were used to estimate per-hecatre biomass, C, N, and C:N ratios, (3) per-hectare estimates of these variables were greater when vegetation control was applied, and (4) estimates of biomass and N content were improved by incorporating a biomass equation into the mean-tree diameter estimation method.

we developed new diameter based allometric biomass equations for individual tree components in an 11 year old Douglas fir stand, and that the equations can be used for estimating per-hectare tree biomass and nutrient content.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of vegetation control in a Douglas-fir plantation.
developing accurate and precise biomass, N, and C estimates in a highly productive plantation.
the influence of vegetation control on biomass and N and C content of Douglas-fir plantation trees, and the accuracy of biomass estimation equations for these trees.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
biomass, C, N, and diameter equations developed for this study can provide accurate and precise estimates of biomass and nutrient content for individual trees and per-hectare totals.

our biomass estimates were more accurate than estimates using previously published equations, and that using mean-tree biomass equations to estimate biomass per hectare was less precise than using allometric equations.
the use of allometric equations to estimate individual-tree biomass, C, or N content is superior to the use of mean-tree biomass equations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

(1) allometric equations for component biomass are not influenced by vegetation control, (2) biomass, C, or N estimates are greater where vegetation control is applied, (3) our biomass equations are not equivalent to published biomass equations, and (4) using the mean-tree diameter method to estimate biomass improves accuracy.

(1) the mean-tree biomass method should not be used for estimating biomass in Douglas-fir plantations on highly productive sites, (2) allometric equations should be used to estimate tree biomass in these plantations, and (3) published allometric equations for Douglas-fir should not be used in plantations on highly fertile sites.
biomass estimates using our diameter-based biomass equations were more precise than those made by other researchers using published biomass equations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the mean-tree biomass method can be used to make accurate estimates of per-hectare C and N content when biomass equations are unavailable for the species of interest.
biomass estimates are more accurate when using diameter based allometric biomass equations rather than the mean-tree approach.
biomass estimates based on allometric equations developed for a specific site and species are more accurate and precise than those derived from equations developed elsewhere.
